::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- organise generated files in an `output/` folder, separate from the raw data;
- write data frames to CSV (`write_csv()`, `write_csv2()`) and Excel (`writexl`, `openxlsx`);
- export to SPSS, Stata and SAS transport files with `haven`;
- save and restore R objects with `saveRDS()`/`readRDS()` and explain when to prefer them to CSV;
- save a ggplot with `ggsave()`, controlling size and resolution.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. Why think about exporting?

At the end of an analysis you have produced something worth keeping: a cleaned dataset, a summary table for a report, a figure for a slide, a fitted model you do not want to re-fit tomorrow. Exporting means choosing:

1. **where** the file goes (a folder),
2. **what format** it has (CSV, Excel, `.rds`, PNG, …),
3. **who** will read it (a person in Excel, a colleague in SPSS, R itself next week).

The third point decides the second. In this lesson, the code that writes files is shown but not run on the website (`eval: false`); run it in your own project.

## 2. Organise your files

A simple project layout keeps raw data safe and generated files easy to find:

```
my-project/
├── my-project.Rproj      (or a .here file)
├── data/                 raw data: never modified by code
├── R/ or scripts/        your .R or .qmd files
└── output/               everything the code creates (tables, figures, .rds)
```

Two rules make this work:

- **Raw data are read-only.** Scripts read from `data/` and write to `output/`. If something goes wrong you can delete `output/` and re-run everything.
- **Paths are project-relative**, built with `here::here()` (see [Importing data](18-import.qmd#files-and-paths)).

Create the output folder from code, so the script works on a fresh copy of the project:

```{r}
#| label: output-dir
#| eval: false
dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

`showWarnings = FALSE` avoids a warning when the folder already exists. Give files informative names (`mpg_by_gear.csv`, not `table1_final_v3.csv`), in lower case and without spaces.

## 3. A table to export

We export a small summary of `mtcars`: the average fuel consumption and displacement by number of gears.

```{r}
#| label: summary-table
by_gear <- mtcars |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mpg  = mean(mpg),
    mean_disp = mean(disp),
    .by = gear
  ) |>
  arrange(gear)

by_gear
```

## 4. CSV files

CSV is the most portable format: any program can read it, and it is plain text, so it works well with version control. Its limits: it stores **no types** (a factor becomes text, a date becomes a string) and only **one table** per file.

### `readr::write_csv()` and `write_csv2()`

```{r}
#| label: write-csv
#| eval: false
write_csv(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.csv"))

# semicolon separator and decimal comma (Excel in many European locales)
write_csv2(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear_eu.csv"))
```

`write_csv()` never writes row names, always uses UTF-8 encoding and writes missing values as `NA` (use `na = ""` for empty cells). If the file is meant to be opened by double-clicking in Excel and contains accented letters, `write_excel_csv()` adds a marker that tells Excel the file is UTF-8.

### Base R: `write.csv()` and `write.csv2()`

```{r}
#| label: write-csv-base
#| eval: false
write.csv(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv2(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear_eu.csv"),
           row.names = FALSE)
```

Without `row.names = FALSE`, base R adds a first column of row numbers (or row names) — the unnamed first column you met when importing `mtcars.csv`. Without a file name, `write.csv()` prints to the console, which is a quick way to see what would be written:

```{r}
#| label: write-console
write.csv(head(by_gear, 2), row.names = FALSE)
```

## 5. Excel files

### Quick: `writexl::write_xlsx()`

`writexl` has no dependencies (no Java, no Excel needed) and does one thing: write data frames to `.xlsx`. A **named list** of data frames becomes a workbook with one sheet per element:

```{r}
#| label: writexl
#| eval: false
writexl::write_xlsx(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.xlsx"))

writexl::write_xlsx(
  list(summary_by_gear = by_gear, raw_data = mtcars),
  here::here("output", "mtcars_export.xlsx")
)
```

### With formatting: `openxlsx`

When the workbook is a deliverable (bold headers, column widths, frozen first row), use `openxlsx`. You build a workbook object step by step and save it at the end:

```{r}
#| label: openxlsx
#| eval: false
wb <- openxlsx::createWorkbook()
openxlsx::addWorksheet(wb, "summary")
openxlsx::writeData(wb, "summary", by_gear,
                    headerStyle = openxlsx::createStyle(textDecoration = "bold"))
openxlsx::setColWidths(wb, "summary", cols = 1:4, widths = "auto")
openxlsx::freezePane(wb, "summary", firstRow = TRUE)
openxlsx::saveWorkbook(wb, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear_formatted.xlsx"),
                       overwrite = TRUE)
```

For a single data frame without formatting, `openxlsx::write.xlsx(by_gear, file, overwrite = TRUE)` is a one-line alternative. (`openxlsx2` is a newer, actively developed successor with a similar purpose and a pipe-friendly interface; the older `xlsx` package requires Java and is best avoided.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel is for people, not for pipelines
Export to Excel when a *person* needs to look at the numbers. If the file will be read again by code, CSV, `.rds` or Parquet are safer: Excel may silently convert values (gene names such as `SEPT2` into dates, long IDs into rounded numbers) when someone opens and re-saves the file.
:::

## 6. SPSS, Stata and SAS

`haven` writes the native formats of SPSS and Stata, and the SAS **transport** format:

```{r}
#| label: haven-write
#| eval: false
haven::write_sav(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.sav"))    # SPSS
haven::write_dta(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.dta"))    # Stata
haven::write_xpt(by_gear, here::here("output", "mpg_by_gear.xpt"))    # SAS
```

- Factors are written as **labelled** integer codes, so SPSS and Stata users see both the codes and the category names.
- Variable names must respect the rules of the target software (for example, Stata names cannot contain dots and are at most 32 characters). `janitor::clean_names()` usually takes care of this.
- For SAS, use `write_xpt()`, which writes a **SAS transport (XPORT)** file that SAS reads reliably (it is also the format required by some regulatory agencies). `haven::write_sas()` (native `.sas7bdat`) is deprecated and its files may not open correctly in SAS.

## 7. R's own formats: `.rds` and `.RData`

### `saveRDS()` / `readRDS()`: one object, exactly as it is

An `.rds` file stores **any single R object** — a data frame, a list, a fitted model — with all its types and attributes:

```{r}
#| label: rds
#| eval: false
saveRDS(by_gear, here::here("output", "by_gear.rds"))

gear_table <- readRDS(here::here("output", "by_gear.rds"))  # any name you like
```

Why does this matter? A CSV round trip **loses types**. Here we write to a temporary file (which R deletes at the end of the session), so the demonstration does not touch any project folder:

```{r}
#| label: roundtrip
peng <- penguins[1:5, c("species", "island", "body_mass")]

tmp_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
tmp_rds <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
write.csv(peng, tmp_csv, row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(peng, tmp_rds)

from_csv <- read.csv(tmp_csv)
from_rds <- readRDS(tmp_rds)

class(from_csv$species)          # text: the factor levels are gone
class(from_rds$species)          # still a factor
identical(from_rds, peng)        # exactly the same object
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output
After the CSV round trip, `species` is `character`: the information that it is a factor with levels `Adelie`, `Chinstrap`, `Gentoo` (in that order, including levels that do not appear in these five rows) is lost. The `.rds` copy is `identical()` to the original. Use `.rds` for intermediate results between your own scripts; use CSV to share data with other programs.
:::

### `save()` / `load()`: several objects at once

```{r}
#| label: rdata
#| eval: false
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
save(by_gear, model, file = here::here("output", "analysis.RData"))

load(here::here("output", "analysis.RData"))   # re-creates by_gear and model
```

`load()` re-creates the objects **with their original names**, silently overwriting any object with the same name in your workspace. For this reason `saveRDS()` is usually preferred: you choose the name when reading. (A list of objects can also be saved with `saveRDS(list(a = a, b = b), ...)`.)

## 8. Parquet: typed, compact, for any language (optional)

**Parquet** is a column-oriented file format used by data tools in R, Python, Spark and databases. It keeps column types (like `.rds`), compresses well, and can be read by many programs (unlike `.rds`). The `arrow` package reads and writes it:

```{r}
#| label: parquet
#| eval: false
arrow::write_parquet(penguins, here::here("output", "penguins.parquet"))
penguins_pq <- arrow::read_parquet(here::here("output", "penguins.parquet"))
```

It is worth considering when files are large (millions of rows) or shared with Python users.

## 9. Saving plots with `ggsave()`

`ggsave()` writes a ggplot to a file; the format follows the file extension (`.png`, `.pdf`, `.svg`, `.jpg`, …).

```{r}
#| label: fig-mass-flipper
#| fig-cap: "Body mass against flipper length for the three penguin species — the figure we save below."
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species")
p
```

```{r}
#| label: ggsave
#| eval: false
ggsave(
  filename = here::here("output", "mass_vs_flipper.png"),
  plot   = p,            # say which plot: do not rely on "the last one shown"
  width  = 16,
  height = 10,
  units  = "cm",
  dpi    = 300           # 300 dots per inch: good for print
)

ggsave(here::here("output", "mass_vs_flipper.pdf"), plot = p,
       width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm")
```

- Always pass `plot =` explicitly. Without it, `ggsave()` saves the **last plot displayed**, which in a long script may not be the one you mean.
- **Set the size** (`width`, `height`, `units`). Otherwise the size of your current plotting window is used, and the result changes from one computer to another.
- **PNG** (raster) with `dpi = 300` is right for documents and slides; **PDF/SVG** (vector) stay sharp at any zoom and are preferred by many journals.
- Text size in the saved file depends on the physical size: a 30 cm wide plot has relatively *smaller* text than a 12 cm one. Choose the size you will actually use.

For base-R graphics, open a device, draw, and close it: `png(file, width = 1600, height = 1000, res = 200)`, then the plotting code, then `dev.off()`.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Overwriting the raw data.** Never write to `data/`. Write to `output/` so the original stays untouched.
2. **An extra column of row numbers.** Base `write.csv()` needs `row.names = FALSE`; `readr::write_csv()` never writes them.
3. **Expecting CSV to remember types.** Factors, dates and labelled values become plain text or numbers. Use `.rds` (R only) or Parquet for typed data.
4. **`load()` overwriting objects silently.** Prefer `saveRDS()` + `x <- readRDS()`.
5. **`ggsave()` without `plot =` and without a size.** You may save the wrong plot at an unpredictable size.
6. **Absolute paths in export code** (`"C:/Users/…/Desktop/out.csv"`). Use `here::here("output", "out.csv")`.
:::

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Your cleaned data contain factors with a specific order of levels and dates. You will continue the analysis in R tomorrow. Which format?

`.rds` with `saveRDS()`: it keeps every type and attribute. (Parquet would also keep them and be readable from Python.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. A colleague uses SAS. Which `haven` function do you use?

`haven::write_xpt()`, which writes a SAS transport file. `write_sas()` is deprecated.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Why write `plot = p` in `ggsave()`?

Without it, `ggsave()` saves the last plot that was displayed, which may not be `p`. Being explicit makes the script reproducible.
:::

## 11. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)

In the browser R runs in a sandbox, so files written to `tempfile()` are safe to create and read back.

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — predict the output.** Without running it, predict how many columns the CSV text below has, and what the first line looks like. Then run it and compare with the version that uses `row.names = FALSE`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_19_1
small <- head(mtcars[, c("mpg", "cyl")], 3)
write.csv(small)
write.csv(small, row.names = ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_19_1"}
`mtcars` has row names (the car models). By default `write.csv()` writes them as an unnamed first column.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_19_1"}
```r
write.csv(small)                     # 3 columns: "", "mpg", "cyl"
write.csv(small, row.names = FALSE)  # 2 columns: "mpg", "cyl"
```
The first version starts with `"","mpg","cyl"` and the car names in the first column. Here the car names are real information, so if you drop row names, first turn them into a proper column: `small$model <- rownames(small)`.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — a round trip that loses information.** Save `chickwts` (where `feed` is a factor) to a temporary CSV file and to a temporary `.rds` file, read both back, and compare the **levels** of `feed`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_19_2
tmp_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
tmp_rds <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
write.csv(chickwts, tmp_csv, row.names = FALSE)
______(chickwts, tmp_rds)

from_csv <- read.csv(tmp_csv)
from_rds <- ______(tmp_rds)

class(from_csv$feed)
levels(from_rds$feed)
identical(from_rds, chickwts)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_19_2"}
Use `saveRDS()` to write and `readRDS()` to read.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_19_2"}
```r
saveRDS(chickwts, tmp_rds)
from_rds <- readRDS(tmp_rds)
class(from_csv$feed)       # "character"
levels(from_rds$feed)      # the six feed types, in their original order
identical(from_rds, chickwts)   # TRUE
```
You could turn `from_csv$feed` back into a factor, but you would have to know (and retype) the level order. The `.rds` file keeps it for you.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — a European CSV.** Write the mean `len` by `supp` and `dose` of `ToothGrowth` to the console in the "European" CSV format (semicolons and decimal commas). Use `aggregate()` to compute the table.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_19_3
tg <- aggregate(len ~ supp + dose, data = ToothGrowth, FUN = mean)
______(tg, row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_19_3"}
The base function for this format is `write.csv2()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_19_3"}
```r
tg <- aggregate(len ~ supp + dose, data = ToothGrowth, FUN = mean)
write.csv2(tg, row.names = FALSE)
```
Each line looks like `"OJ";0,5;13,23`: `;` separates values and `,` is the decimal mark. With `readr` loaded, `write_csv2()` does the same.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — a small report folder.** In a project of your own: create `output/`, compute the mean body mass by species and sex of `penguins` (dropping missing values), and save (a) the table as CSV and as an Excel file with one sheet for the table and one for the raw data, and (b) a boxplot of body mass by species as a 15 × 10 cm PNG at 300 dpi.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)

mass_tab <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex), !is.na(body_mass)) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass), n = n(), .by = c(species, sex))

write_csv(mass_tab, here::here("output", "mass_by_species_sex.csv"))
writexl::write_xlsx(
  list(summary = mass_tab, raw = penguins),
  here::here("output", "penguins_mass.xlsx")
)

p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(species, body_mass)) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)")
ggsave(here::here("output", "mass_boxplot.png"), plot = p,
       width = 15, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
```
Delete the `output/` folder and re-run the script: everything is re-created. That is the test of a reproducible workflow.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — to SPSS and back.** Write `penguins` to an SPSS file with `haven::write_sav()`, read it back with `read_sav()`, and compare the class of `species` before and after. Convert it back to a factor and check that the levels are the same as in the original.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
library(haven)
path <- here::here("output", "penguins.sav")
write_sav(penguins, path)
back <- read_sav(path)

class(penguins$species)   # "factor"
class(back$species)       # "haven_labelled" ...: codes 1, 2, 3 with labels

back$species <- as_factor(back$species)
identical(levels(back$species), levels(penguins$species))   # TRUE
```
SPSS has no factor type: it stores numbers with value labels. `as_factor()` rebuilds the factor from those labels.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Goal | Function | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Output folder | `dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)` | never write into `data/` |
| CSV | `readr::write_csv()`, `write.csv(row.names = FALSE)` | portable, no types |
| CSV for European Excel | `readr::write_csv2()`, `write.csv2()` | `;` and decimal comma |
| Excel, quick | `writexl::write_xlsx(df_or_named_list, path)` | one sheet per list element |
| Excel, formatted | `openxlsx::createWorkbook()` … `saveWorkbook()` | styles, widths, frozen panes |
| SPSS / Stata / SAS | `haven::write_sav()`, `write_dta()`, `write_xpt()` | `write_sas()` is deprecated |
| One R object | `saveRDS()` / `readRDS()` | keeps all types |
| Several R objects | `save()` / `load()` | `load()` can overwrite objects |
| Large typed data, any language | `arrow::write_parquet()` | optional |
| Plots | `ggsave(file, plot = p, width, height, units, dpi)` | always set `plot` and size |

- Keep **raw data read-only** and write everything to **`output/`** with project-relative paths.
- Choose the format by **who reads it next**: people (Excel, CSV), other software (CSV, SPSS/Stata/XPT, Parquet), R (`.rds`).
- CSV is portable but **forgets types**; `.rds` remembers everything.
- Save plots with an **explicit plot and size**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
